fixed.q: I. The largest four-digit number in base 7 is 7777. II. The smallest four-digit number in base 8 is 1111. Which is correct?
fixed.w: Base-b digits are 0 to b−1: largest 4-digit base-7 = 6666; smallest 4-digit base-8 = 1000.

fixed.q: The radix (base) of a number system equals:
o: The number of distinct symbols it uses
The number of bits per digit
fixed.w: Binary 2 symbols, octal 8, decimal 10, hex 16 (A–F = 10–15).

fixed.q: Converting binary to octal and hexadecimal, the bits are grouped (from the binary point outwards) in groups of:
fixed.w: Groups of 2 for base 4, 3 for base 8, 4 for base 16. Between base 4, 8 and 16 go through binary.

fixed.q: To convert a decimal FRACTION to binary, you:
o: Multiply repeatedly by 2 and read the integer parts top to bottom
Divide repeatedly by 2 and read remainders bottom to top
Multiply by 2 and read the integer parts bottom to top
Divide by 2 and read remainders top to bottom
fixed.w: Integer part: divide, read remainders bottom-up. Fraction: multiply, read integer parts top-down. 10.25 → 1010.01.

fixed.q: If (11A1B)₈ = (12C9)₁₆, the values of A and B are:
A decimal number with 25 digits needs approximately how many bits in binary?
fixed.w: bits ≈ digits × log₂10 = 25 × 3.32 ≈ 83. (The 2017 paper had no 83 and its key picked the closest option, 74.)

fixed.q: Regarding the sign bit: I. 0 means positive. II. 1 means negative. Which is correct?
fixed.w: MSB = sign bit in signed representations.

fixed.q: Which signed representation has only ONE representation of zero?
fixed.w: Sign-magnitude and 1's complement both have +0 and −0.

fixed.q: The range of an n-bit 2's-complement number is:
fixed.w: 8 bits: −128 to +127. Sign-magnitude and 1's complement: −127 to +127. Unsigned: 0 to 255.

fixed.q: In 4 bits, −5 is written in sign-magnitude, 1's complement and 2's complement respectively as:
Dividing a signed (2's-complement) binary number by 2 is done by:
o: Arithmetic right shift (copying the sign bit in)
fixed.w: Shift right = ÷2, shift left = ×2. Arithmetic shift keeps the sign. (A 2023 PYQ called it '3's complement' and keyed 10100 → 01010, a logical right shift.)

fixed.q: To compute A − B using 2's complement, you:
o: Add A to the 2's complement of B and discard the end carry
Add A to the 1's complement of B and discard the carry
Add the 2's complements of both A and B
fixed.w: If there is no end carry, the result is negative and in 2's-complement form.

fixed.q: A code in which only one bit changes between successive numbers is:
fixed.w: Gray code is also called the minimum-error (unit-distance, reflected binary) code.

fixed.q: Which of the following is the minimum-error code?
fixed.w: Only one bit changes at a time, so a transition can be misread by at most one bit.

fixed.q: Which of these is a self-complementing code?
fixed.w: Excess-3 = BCD + 0011; the code of 9 − d is the complement of the code of d (2421 is also self-complementing).

fixed.q: Which pair are non-weighted codes?
fixed.w: Weighted: 8421 BCD, 2421. Non-weighted: Excess-3, Gray.

fixed.q: How many of the 16 four-bit combinations are INVALID in BCD?
fixed.w: 1010 to 1111 (10–15) are unused.

fixed.q: Binary to Gray conversion: the MSB is kept and each next Gray bit is:
o: The XOR of that binary bit with the binary bit to its left
The AND of adjacent binary bits
The complement of the binary bit
The XOR of the Gray bit just produced and the next binary bit
fixed.w: Gray → binary is the reverse: each binary bit = previous BINARY bit ⊕ current Gray bit.

fixed.q: Standard ASCII and extended ASCII use, respectively:
fixed.w: Extended ASCII uses 8 bits.

fixed.q: ASCII can handle only ___ or at most ___ languages, which shows its limitation.
fixed.w: English plus at most one more.

fixed.q: Which code gives a unique number for every character of every written language, independent of device, OS or application?
fixed.w: Unicode is the standard meant to cover all the world's languages.

fixed.q: The most commonly used Unicode encoding scheme is:
fixed.w: Unicode encodings: UTF-8 (8-bit units, most common), UTF-16, UTF-32.

fixed.q: In IEEE 754 single precision, the sign, exponent and mantissa bits and the bias are:
fixed.w: Double: 1, 11, 52, bias 1023. Value = (−1)^S × 1.M × 2^(E−bias); the leading 1 is implicit.

fixed.q: In IEEE 754 single precision, exponent field all 1s (255) with a non-zero mantissa represents:
A Hamming code (single-error-correcting) places parity bits at positions:
fixed.w: Number of parity bits p must satisfy 2^p ≥ m + p + 1. A single parity bit only detects odd numbers of bit errors.

fixed.q: Which logic family is the fastest, and which has the lowest power consumption?
fixed.w: Fan-out = the number of gate inputs one output can drive.

fixed.q: I. Boolean algebra facilitates the analysis and design of digital circuits. II. It expresses the input–output relationship of a logic diagram in algebraic form. Which is correct?
The OR-distributive law of Boolean algebra (with no counterpart in ordinary algebra) is:
fixed.w: Used for PYQ: xy + x'z = (x + x')(x + z)(y + x')(y + z) = (x' + y)(x + z)(y + z).

fixed.q: Using the distributive law, F = xy + x'z equals:
fixed.w: Product-of-sums via x + yz = (x + y)(x + z).

fixed.q: x + x'y simplifies to:
fixed.w: Absorption family: x + xy = x; x(x + y) = x; x + x'y = x + y; x(x' + y) = xy.

fixed.q: A + A'B + A'B'C simplifies to:
fixed.w: Apply x + x'y = x + y twice.

fixed.q: By the consensus theorem, AB + A'C + BC equals:
fixed.w: BC is the consensus term and is redundant.

fixed.q: (A + B)(A + B') simplifies to:
fixed.w: Dual of AB + AB' = A.

fixed.q: The dual of a Boolean expression is obtained by:
o: Swapping AND ↔ OR and 0 ↔ 1, leaving variables unchanged
Swapping AND ↔ OR and complementing every variable
fixed.w: Complement of a function = dual + complement every variable.

fixed.q: The complement of the XNOR function xy + x'y' is:
fixed.w: De Morgan: (xy)'(x'y')' = (x' + y')(x + y) = x'y + xy'.

fixed.q: (A ⊕ B ⊕ C)' equals:
fixed.w: Complementing an odd chain of XORs turns one XOR into XNOR. Note A ⊙ B ⊙ C equals A ⊕ B ⊕ C itself (for three variables), so it is NOT the complement.

fixed.q: The total number of distinct Boolean functions of n variables is:
fixed.w: 2 variables → 16; 3 variables → 256. (In the 2017 SSC paper none of the options matched, so 'None of these'.)

fixed.q: The number of Boolean functions of 3 variables with f(X, Y, Z) = f(X', Y', Z') is:
fixed.w: The 8 minterms form 4 complementary pairs that must take the same value: 2⁴ = 16. (Self-dual functions of n variables are also 2^(2ⁿ⁻¹).)

fixed.q: The degree of the term A'B'C'D' is:
fixed.w: Degree = number of literals.

fixed.q: Which function is self-dual?
fixed.w: Its dual (A + B)(B + C)(C + A) simplifies back to AB + BC + CA (the majority function).

fixed.q: SOP and POS forms are built from the truth-table rows where the output is, respectively:
fixed.w: SOP = OR of minterms (output 1); POS = AND of maxterms (output 0).

fixed.q: For variables a, b, c, the input 101 corresponds to:
o: Minterm ab'c and maxterm a' + b + c'
Minterm a'bc' and maxterm a + b' + c
Minterm ab'c and maxterm a + b' + c
Minterm abc and maxterm a' + b' + c'
fixed.w: Minterm: 0 → complemented. Maxterm: 1 → complemented.

fixed.q: Which algebraic function represents a NAND gate?
fixed.w: NOR = (x + y)'.

fixed.q: I. An AND gate gives 1 only if both inputs are 1. II. The AND symbol is the same as multiplication in ordinary arithmetic. Which is correct?
An OR-shaped gate symbol with an extra curved line on the input side is:
fixed.w: A bubble at the output would make it NOR/XNOR.

fixed.q: A 2-way staircase switch: light is ON when exactly one switch is ON, OFF when both are ON or both OFF. Which gate implements it?
fixed.w: Output 1 when inputs differ.

fixed.q: A railway crossing with 4 tracks must close if a train is on at least one track. Which gate?
fixed.w: Any input 1 → output 1.

fixed.q: The input–output relationship of each gate shown in tabular form is a:
Which gates are universal?
fixed.w: Any circuit can be built from NAND alone or NOR alone.

fixed.q: How many NOR gates are needed to make an AND gate?
fixed.w: NOR: NOT 1, OR 2, AND 3, NAND 4, XNOR 4, XOR 5. NAND: NOT 1, AND 2, OR 3, NOR 4, XOR 4, XNOR 5.

fixed.q: The minimum number of 2-input NAND gates needed to build an XOR gate is:
fixed.w: G1 = (AB)', G2 = (A·G1)', G3 = (B·G1)', Y = (G2·G3)'. NOR builds XNOR in 4.

fixed.q: An AND gate with BOTH inputs inverted (bubbled) is equivalent to:
fixed.w: A'·B' = (A + B)'. An OR with bubbled inputs = NAND.

fixed.q: A two-level SOP (AND–OR) circuit converts directly to which all-universal-gate form?
fixed.w: POS (OR–AND) → NOR–NOR.

fixed.q: For a multi-input XOR gate, the output is 1 when:
o: An odd number of inputs are 1
An even number of inputs are 1
fixed.w: So XOR is the odd-parity detector. A ⊕ 0 = A, A ⊕ 1 = A', A ⊕ A = 0.

fixed.q: Why are K-map rows and columns labelled in the order 00, 01, 11, 10?
o: It is Gray-code order, so adjacent cells differ in exactly one variable
It reduces the number of cells
It places don't-cares at the edges
fixed.w: In a 4-variable map the columns read m0, m1, m3, m2.

fixed.q: In a 4-variable K-map, a group (octet) of 8 adjacent 1s produces a term with how many literals?
fixed.w: A group of 2^k cells removes k variables: pair → 3 literals, quad → 2, octet → 1, all 16 → F = 1.

fixed.q: Which K-map cells are adjacent in a 4-variable map?
o: Edge cells wrap around, and the four corners form a group
Only cells in the same row
fixed.w: Left touches right, top touches bottom; no diagonal grouping.

fixed.q: An essential prime implicant is:
o: A prime implicant that covers at least one 1 that no other prime implicant covers
The largest group on the map
A group that includes a don't-care
fixed.w: Every EPI must appear in the minimal expression.

fixed.q: Don't-care conditions in a K-map are:
o: Treated as 1 only if they make a group bigger, otherwise ignored
fixed.w: E.g. BCD inputs 1010–1111 can be don't-cares.

fixed.q: Minimise f(A, B, C) = Σm(0, 2, 5, 7).
fixed.w: m0, m2 wrap (A'C'); m5, m7 (AC).

fixed.q: For a half adder:
fixed.w: It cannot add a carry-in, so it is 'half'.

fixed.q: For a full adder, Carry = ?
fixed.w: Sum = A ⊕ B ⊕ C = Σm(1, 2, 4, 7). Carry = Σm(3, 5, 6, 7) = AB + C(A ⊕ B).

fixed.q: How many AND, OR and XOR gates are needed to implement a full adder directly?
fixed.w: Carry = AB + BC + CA → 3 AND + 2 OR (2-input); Sum → 2 XOR.

fixed.q: A full adder can be built from:
o: Two half adders and one OR gate
Two half adders and one AND gate
One half adder and one XOR gate
fixed.w: HA1 gives A⊕B and AB; HA2 adds Cin; OR the two carries.

fixed.q: For a half subtractor (A − B), the borrow is:
fixed.w: Difference = A ⊕ B. Full subtractor borrow = A'B + A'Bin + B·Bin (A complemented, unlike the adder carry).

fixed.q: The main drawback of a ripple-carry adder is:
o: The carry propagation delay grows with the number of bits
It uses too many XOR gates
fixed.w: Carry look-ahead fixes this by generating all carries at once (faster, more hardware).

fixed.q: In a carry look-ahead adder, the generate and propagate terms are:
fixed.w: Ci+1 = Gi + PiCi; Si = Pi ⊕ Ci.

fixed.q: In a BCD adder, when the 4-bit sum exceeds 9 or produces a carry, the correction is to:
fixed.w: Correction condition C = K + Z3Z2 + Z3Z1.

fixed.q: How many invalid input combinations occur at the input of a BCD adder (two 4-bit digits)?
fixed.w: 2⁸ = 256 combinations; valid 10 × 10 = 100; invalid = 156.

fixed.q: In a 4-bit adder–subtractor, the XOR gate on each B input with mode M = 1 and C0 = 1 makes the circuit compute:
fixed.w: M = 1 inverts B and C0 = 1 adds 1, giving A + B' + 1 = A − B.

fixed.q: A multiplexer with 2ⁿ data inputs has:
fixed.w: MUX = data selector (many to one). DEMUX = 1 to 2ⁿ with n selects.

fixed.q: The output of a 4×1 MUX is:
Advantages of multiplexers: I. Logic design is simplified. II. IC package count is reduced. III. Simplification of the logic expression is not required. Which are correct?
fixed.w: A function can be implemented on a MUX straight from its truth table.

fixed.q: The number of 2-input multiplexers needed to build a 2¹⁰-input multiplexer is:
fixed.w: 2ⁿ × 1 from 2 × 1 MUXes = 2ⁿ − 1.

fixed.q: An n-to-2ⁿ decoder:
o: Activates exactly one output, each output being one minterm of the inputs
Selects one of 2ⁿ inputs onto one output
Produces the binary code of the active input
Has n select lines and 1 output
fixed.w: Any n-variable function = decoder + OR gates on its minterms.

fixed.q: Implementing a full adder with a 3-to-8 decoder needs:
o: Two OR gates: Sum = m1 + m2 + m4 + m7, Carry = m3 + m5 + m6 + m7
One OR gate for Sum only
fixed.w: OR the decoder outputs that correspond to each function's minterms.

fixed.q: An 8-to-3 encoder (octal to binary) is made with three ___ gates.
In a priority encoder, when several inputs are 1 at once:
o: The output is the code of the highest-priority active input, and a valid bit shows some input is active
The output is the OR of all active codes
fixed.w: 4×2 priority encoder (D3 highest): A1 = D3 + D2, A0 = D3 + D2'D1, V = D3 + D2 + D1 + D0.

fixed.q: For a 1-bit magnitude comparator, the A = B output is:
fixed.w: A > B → AB'; A < B → A'B.

fixed.q: A sequential circuit differs from a combinational circuit because its output depends on:
o: Present inputs and the past state (memory)
fixed.w: Sequential = combinational + memory (feedback).

fixed.q: i) A clock signal is required for sequential circuits. ii) Memory elements are required in a sequential circuit. As per the exam key:
fixed.w: Asynchronous sequential circuits exist, but the key treats both as true (for synchronous circuits).

fixed.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a latch from a flip-flop?
o: A latch is level-sensitive/unclocked; a flip-flop changes state only at the clock (edge)
A latch stores 2 bits; a flip-flop stores 1
A latch needs a clock edge
fixed.w: A flip-flop is a 1-bit memory cell, also called a bistable multivibrator.

fixed.q: I. Astable multivibrator – flip-flop. II. Bistable multivibrator – free running. Which pairing is correct?
fixed.w: Astable = free running (no stable state); monostable = one stable state; bistable = flip-flop.

fixed.q: In an SR latch built from NOR gates, which input combination is invalid?
fixed.w: In the NAND latch (active-low inputs) the invalid combination is S' = R' = 0.

fixed.q: The characteristic equation of the SR flip-flop is:
fixed.w: JK: JQ' + K'Q. T: T ⊕ Q. D: D.

fixed.q: The characteristic equation of the JK flip-flop is:
fixed.w: JK = 11 toggles; 00 holds; 01 resets; 10 sets.

fixed.q: The characteristic equation of the T flip-flop is:
fixed.w: T = 1 toggles (divides frequency by 2).

fixed.q: In the JK excitation table, the transition Qn = 0 → Qn+1 = 1 needs:
In the SR excitation table, the transition Qn = 1 → Qn+1 = 1 needs:
For a T flip-flop, which transitions require T = 1?
fixed.w: T = 1 whenever the state changes. For D, D = Qn+1.

fixed.q: The race-around condition in a JK flip-flop occurs when:
o: J = K = 1 and the clock pulse width is longer than the propagation delay
fixed.w: The output keeps toggling while the clock is high. Fixes: edge triggering or master–slave JK.

fixed.q: In a master–slave JK flip-flop:
o: The master is enabled when CLK = 1 and the slave when CLK = 0
Only the master has J and K inputs connected to the clock
fixed.w: The output changes once per clock pulse, removing race-around.

fixed.q: Which flip-flop is used to make all types of shift registers?
fixed.w: D (data/delay): Qn+1 = D.

fixed.q: To convert an SR flip-flop into a D flip-flop, the input logic is:
fixed.w: Same idea for JK → D: J = D, K = D'.

fixed.q: To convert a JK flip-flop into a T flip-flop:
fixed.w: Tie J and K together to T: T = 0 gives J = K = 0 (hold), T = 1 gives J = K = 1 (toggle), exactly the T flip-flop.

fixed.q: To convert a T flip-flop into a JK flip-flop, T = ?
fixed.w: Check: J = K = 1 → T = Qn' + Qn = 1 → toggles.

fixed.q: To convert a D flip-flop into a T flip-flop, D = ?
fixed.w: Conversely T → D: T = D ⊕ Qn. D → JK: D = JQn' + K'Qn.

fixed.q: To convert an SR flip-flop into a JK flip-flop:
fixed.w: SR → T: S = TQn', R = TQn. JK → SR: J = S, K = R.

fixed.q: A flip-flop symbol with a triangle AND a bubble at the clock input is:
fixed.w: Triangle alone = positive edge (0 → 1).

fixed.q: A device that stores (and sometimes displays) the number of times an event has occurred, relative to a clock, is a:
A mod-6 counter and a mod-8 counter in cascade give a:
fixed.w: Cascaded moduli multiply.

fixed.q: A counter in which the output of one flip-flop drives the clock input of the next is a:
fixed.w: In a ripple counter the external clock goes to the first FF only.

fixed.q: In a ripple counter using edge-triggered JK flip-flops, the pulse input is applied to the:
o: Clock input of one (the first) flip-flop
J and K inputs of one flip-flop
J and K inputs of all flip-flops

fixed.q: Compared with a ripple counter, a synchronous counter is:
o: Faster, since all flip-flops share one clock, but needs more logic
Unable to count in arbitrary sequences
fixed.w: Ripple delay = n × tpd; synchronous delay = one FF + gate delay. Synchronous counters can follow any sequence.

fixed.q: A ripple counter made of NEGATIVE-edge-triggered flip-flops, each clocked from the previous stage's Q output, counts:
fixed.w: Negative edge + Q → up; negative edge + Q' → down. Positive edge reverses this.

fixed.q: Four D flip-flops on a common clock, each with its own input line and its own output line, form a:
Shifting the contents of a binary register one place to the LEFT:
fixed.w: Shift right divides by 2.

fixed.q: A universal (bidirectional) shift register can:
o: Shift left, shift right and load in parallel, chosen by mode-control lines
fixed.w: Example IC: 74194. Uses: SISO = delay; SIPO = serial→parallel; PISO = parallel→serial; PIPO = buffer.

fixed.q: Which counter is a shift register whose complemented output of the last stage is fed to the D input of the first stage?
fixed.w: A ring counter feeds back Q (not Q').

fixed.q: With n flip-flops, a ring counter and a Johnson counter have how many states respectively?
fixed.w: Unused states: ring 2ⁿ − n; Johnson 2ⁿ − 2n (a 4-bit Johnson counter has 8 unused).

fixed.q: ______ has been developed to incorporate all the character of every written language of the world. It provides a unique number for every character, irrespective of device [server, desktop, mob], OS [linux, win] or software application
fixed.w: Unicode gives a unique number to every character of every script, independent of platform, OS or application.

fixed.q: Unicode in the programming language can be represented using which of the bit format standards in computer science?
fixed.w: Unicode is commonly represented with the 8-bit UTF-8 format (also UTF-16 and UTF-32).

fixed.q: Represent (743)₈ in Gray code.
fixed.w: (743)₈ = 111 100 011. Gray code: g = b₁, then bᵢ XOR bᵢ₋₁, giving 100010010.

fixed.q: A register contains a 3's complement number 10100. If it is divided by 2, find the value of the register.
fixed.w: 01010 (logical right shift). The question is flawed: '3's complement' should be 2's complement, and an arithmetic shift of 10100 would give 11010.

fixed.q: What is the binary equivalent of the decimal number 10.25?
The decimal equivalent of the binary number 111111 is:
If (21121)₃ = (C)₄, then what is the value of C?
(84)₁₂ = (?)₈ (bases as reconstructed from the garbled source)
Which of the following statements is true?
o: Extended ASCII uses 8 bits for coding.
Extended ASCII uses 9 bits for coding.
Extended ASCII uses 10 bits for coding.
Extended ASCII uses 11 bits for coding.
fixed.w: Standard ASCII is 7-bit (128 codes). Extended ASCII uses the full 8-bit byte (256 codes).

fixed.q: A decimal number has 25 digits. The number of bits needed for its equivalent binary representation is approximately
fixed.w: Bits ≈ 25 × log2(10) = 25 × 3.32 ≈ 83. No option matches exactly; B (74) is the closest listed. Treat this as a flawed question.

fixed.q: The ______ standard promises to provide enough characters to cover all the world's languages.
fixed.w: Unicode aims to cover the characters of all the world's scripts.

fixed.q: Addition of 1101₂ and 1000₂ is
The hexadecimal equivalent of (101010011011)₂ is
Octal equivalent of (111101000)₂ is
Using K-map, simplify the Boolean function: F(x, y, z) = S (0, 2, 4, 5, 6) Which of the following is simplified function?
fixed.w: Minterms 0, 2, 4, 6 group to z'; minterms 4 and 5 group to xy'. So F = z' + xy'.

fixed.q: Which statement(s) is/are correct regarding the Boolean algebra? I. It facilitate the analysis and design of digital circuits. II. Expresses in algebraic form the input-output relationship of logic diagram.
fixed.w: Boolean algebra is used to analyse and design digital circuits and expresses their input–output relationship algebraically. Both are true.

fixed.q: The total number of possible Boolean functions involving 'n' Boolean variables will be
fixed.w: A truth table on n variables has 2^n rows and each row can be 0 or 1, so there are 2^(2^n) functions. None of the listed options matches.

fixed.q: For what minimum value of propagation delay in each FF will a 10-bit ripple counter skip a count when it is clocked at 10 MHz?
fixed.w: A ripple counter's total delay is 10 × t_pd. It skips a count when this reaches the 100 ns clock period, i.e. t_pd = 10 ns.

fixed.q: The given diagram expresses ______. [Diagram: four D flip-flops on a common clock, each with its own input line from the top (INPUTS) and its own output line at the bottom (OUTPUTS)]
fixed.w: Each flip-flop has its own parallel input and its own parallel output, so this is Parallel-In Parallel-Out (PIPO).

fixed.q: Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct regarding AND logic gate? I. The AND gate produces the output value 1 if input A and input B are both equal to 1. II. The algebraic operation symbol of the AND function is the same as the multiplication symbol of ordinary arithmetic.
fixed.w: AND outputs 1 only when both inputs are 1, and it is written like multiplication (A·B). Both are true.

fixed.q: A 2 way switch works as follows: Both switches ON = lights off Both switches OFF = light off One switch ON and other OFF = light on Which gate can be used to implement this?
fixed.w: The light is on only when the switches differ, which is the XOR truth table.

fixed.q: Which of the following is an advantage of use of multiplexers? I. Logic design is simplified II. Minimizes IC package count III. Simplification of logic expression is not required
fixed.w: A multiplexer simplifies logic design, reduces IC package count and needs no prior simplification of the expression. All three are advantages.

fixed.q: The BCD (8421) code of decimal 59 is:
fixed.w: Each decimal digit becomes 4 bits: 5 = 0101, 9 = 1001.

fixed.q: Which BCD groups are invalid?
fixed.w: BCD uses only 0000–1001 (0–9).

fixed.q: The excess-3 code of decimal 4 is:
fixed.w: Add 3 to each digit: 4 + 3 = 7 = 0111.

fixed.q: Which code is self-complementing?
fixed.w: The 9's complement of a digit is the 1's complement of its excess-3 code (2421 is also self-complementing).

fixed.q: The Gray code of binary 1011 is:
fixed.w: Keep the MSB, then XOR each pair of adjacent bits: 1, 1⊕0 = 1, 0⊕1 = 1, 1⊕1 = 0.

fixed.q: The main property of Gray code is that:
o: Successive values differ in only one bit
fixed.w: This is why it is used in shaft encoders and K-map ordering.

fixed.q: ASCII is a ___-bit code and can represent ___ characters.
fixed.w: Extended ASCII uses 8 bits (256); Unicode is much larger.

fixed.q: An even-parity bit for data 1011001 is:
fixed.w: The data has four 1s (already even), so the parity bit is 0.

fixed.q: Which gates are called universal gates?
fixed.w: Any Boolean function can be built using only NAND or only NOR gates.

fixed.q: The output of an XOR gate is 1 when:
fixed.w: XNOR is 1 when the inputs are equal (equality detector).

fixed.q: (1101.101)₂ in decimal is:
(2F)₁₆ in decimal is:
(745)₈ in binary is:
fixed.w: Each octal digit becomes 3 bits.

fixed.q: De Morgan's theorem states that (A + B)' equals:
fixed.w: Also (A·B)' = A' + B'.

fixed.q: A mod-10 counter needs at least how many flip-flops?
fixed.w: 2ⁿ ≥ 10 gives n = 4. Cascading mod-M and mod-N counters gives mod-(M×N).

fixed.q: In a ripple (asynchronous) counter:
o: Each flip-flop is clocked by the previous flip-flop's output
fixed.w: Delays add up from stage to stage, so ripple counters are slower than synchronous ones.

fixed.q: A ring counter with n flip-flops has how many states?
fixed.w: A Johnson (twisted-ring) counter has 2n states.

fixed.q: The 2's complement of 0110 is:
fixed.w: Invert the bits (1001) and add 1.

fixed.q: IEEE 754 double precision uses:
fixed.w: Its exponent bias is 1023.

fixed.q: The exponent bias in IEEE 754 double precision is:
fixed.w: Bias = 2^(k-1) - 1 with k = 11 exponent bits.

fixed.q: In a normalised IEEE 754 number, the bit before the binary point of the mantissa is:
o: An implicit 1 that is not stored
Stored as the first mantissa bit
fixed.w: The hidden bit gives one extra bit of precision.

fixed.q: In IEEE 754 single precision, the stored (biased) exponent of 5.0 is:

theory.Number systems:
• Base b uses digits 0 … b−1 (largest 4-digit base-7 number 6666; smallest 4-digit base-8 number 1000).
• Any base → decimal: Σ digit × b^position.
• Decimal → base b: integer part divide repeatedly, remainders bottom-up; fraction multiply repeatedly, integer parts top-down.
• Binary ↔ octal: groups of 3 bits; ↔ hex: groups of 4, from the binary point outwards. Between 4/8/16 go through binary.
• Digits needed: d decimal digits ≈ 3.32·d bits.
• Addition in base b: carry when a column reaches b.
theory.Signed numbers:
• MSB is the sign bit (0 +, 1 −).
• 1's complement = flip all bits. 2's complement = 1's + 1 (shortcut: copy up to the first 1 from the right, flip the rest).
• Ranges (n bits): unsigned 0 … 2ⁿ−1; sign-magnitude and 1's ±(2ⁿ⁻¹−1) with two zeros; 2's −2ⁿ⁻¹ … 2ⁿ⁻¹−1 with one zero.
• Read a 2's-complement number: MSB weight −2ⁿ⁻¹.
• A − B = A + 2's(B), discard the end carry.
• Arithmetic shift right = ÷2 (copy sign bit); shift left = ×2.
theory.Codes:
• Weighted: BCD 8421, 2421. Non-weighted: Excess-3 (BCD + 0011), Gray.
• BCD: 6 invalid codes (1010–1111). Self-complementing: Excess-3, 2421.
• Gray: one bit changes between successive values (minimum-error code). Binary→Gray: keep MSB, gᵢ = bᵢ ⊕ bᵢ₋₁(left). Gray→binary: keep MSB, bᵢ = bᵢ₋₁ ⊕ gᵢ.
• ASCII 7-bit (128); extended ASCII 8-bit (256); ASCII handles 1, at most 2 languages. Unicode covers all languages; UTF-8 most common (also UTF-16, UTF-32).
theory.Floating point:
• IEEE 754 single: 1 sign, 8 exponent, 23 mantissa, bias 127. Double: 1, 11, 52, bias 1023.
• Value = (−1)^S × 1.M × 2^(E − bias); the leading 1 is implicit.
• E all 0s: zero (M = 0) or denormal; E all 1s: ∞ (M = 0) or NaN.
theory.Error codes:
• Parity bit: detects odd numbers of bit errors.
• Hamming: parity bits at positions 1, 2, 4, 8 …; 2^p ≥ m + p + 1; corrects 1-bit, detects 2-bit errors.
theory.Logic families: • ECL fastest; CMOS lowest power; TTL bipolar, 5 V. Fan-out = number of inputs one output can drive.
theory.Boolean algebra:
• Laws: idempotent, commutative, associative, distributive (x + yz = (x + y)(x + z)), De Morgan ((xy)' = x' + y', (x + y)' = x'y'), absorption (x + xy = x, x + x'y = x + y), consensus (AB + A'C + BC = AB + A'C).
• Dual: swap AND↔OR and 0↔1, keep variables. Complement: dual + complement each variable. Self-dual example: AB + BC + CA.
• Count: 2ⁿ rows; 2^(2ⁿ) functions; 2^(2ⁿ⁻¹) self-dual functions.
• XOR facts: A⊕0 = A, A⊕1 = A', A⊕A = 0; (A⊕B⊕C)' = A⊕B⊙C; three-variable A⊙B⊙C = A⊕B⊕C.
• Degree of a term = number of literals.
theory.SOP/POS:
• SOP from rows with output 1 (OR of minterms Σm); POS from rows with output 0 (AND of maxterms ΠM).
• Minterm: 0 → complemented variable. Maxterm: 1 → complemented variable.
• Σm and ΠM of the same function use complementary index sets.
• Canonical form: expand missing variables with (v + v').
theory.Gates:
• AND (1 only if all 1), OR (0 only if all 0), NAND = (AB)', NOR = (A + B)', XOR = A'B + AB' (1 when inputs differ / odd number of 1s), XNOR = equality.
• Universal: NAND, NOR. NAND counts: NOT 1, AND 2, OR 3, NOR 4, XOR 4, XNOR 5. NOR counts: NOT 1, OR 2, AND 3, NAND 4, XNOR 4, XOR 5.
• Bubbled-input AND = NOR; bubbled-input OR = NAND.
• SOP → NAND–NAND; POS → NOR–NOR.
• Truth table shows the input–output relationship.
theory.K-map:
• Cells in Gray order 00, 01, 11, 10 (4-var columns: m0 m1 m3 m2; rows 00 01 11 10).
• Group 1s (SOP) or 0s (POS) in rectangles of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16; edges wrap, four corners form a group; no diagonals; groups as large and as few as possible.
• A group of 2^k cells drops k variables (4-var: pair → 3 literals, quad → 2, octet → 1).
• Read a group: keep variables that are constant across it (SOP: 0 → x', 1 → x; POS: 0 → x, 1 → x').
• Don't cares: use only if they enlarge a group. Essential prime implicant: covers a 1 no other PI covers.
theory.Adders:
• Half adder: S = A⊕B, C = AB. Full adder: S = A⊕B⊕Cin, Cout = AB + BC + CA = AB + Cin(A⊕B); built from 2 HAs + 1 OR; direct form 3 AND, 2 OR, 2 XOR.
• Half subtractor: D = A⊕B, borrow = A'B. Full subtractor borrow = A'B + A'Bin + B·Bin.
• Ripple carry: delay grows with n. Worst case ≈ (n − 1)·t_carry + t_sum.
• CLA: Gi = AiBi, Pi = Ai⊕Bi, Ci+1 = Gi + PiCi; faster, more hardware.
• BCD adder: if sum > 9 or carry, add 0110. Invalid inputs: 256 − 100 = 156.
• Adder–subtractor: XOR each B with M; M = 1 and C0 = 1 gives A − B.
theory.MUX/Decoder:
• MUX: 2ⁿ inputs, n select lines, 1 output (data selector). 4×1: Y = S1'S0'I0 + S1'S0I1 + S1S0'I2 + S1S0I3.
• 2ⁿ×1 MUX from 2×1 MUXes: 2ⁿ − 1 (2¹⁰ → 1023). Build level by level: N/k + N/k² + … + 1.
• MUX advantages: simpler design, fewer ICs, no K-map simplification needed.
• DEMUX: 1 input → 2ⁿ outputs. Decoder: n → 2ⁿ, each output a minterm; decoder + OR gates realise any function (full adder: two ORs).
• Encoder 2ⁿ → n made of OR gates (8×3 uses 3 ORs). Priority encoder: highest active input wins, valid bit V.
• Comparator: A>B = AB', A<B = A'B, A=B = A⊙B.
theory.Sequential:
• Sequential = combinational + memory; output depends on inputs and past state. (Exam key: clock and memory both required.)
• Synchronous changes on clock; asynchronous on input change.
• Latch: level-sensitive/unclocked. Flip-flop: clocked 1-bit memory = bistable multivibrator. Astable = free running; monostable = one stable state.
theory.Flip-flops:
• SR (NOR latch): 11 invalid; NAND latch: 00 invalid. Q+ = S + R'Q (SR = 0).
• JK: 00 hold, 01 reset, 10 set, 11 toggle; Q+ = JQ' + K'Q.
• T: Q+ = T⊕Q (T = 1 toggles). D: Q+ = D (used in all shift registers).
• Excitation (Q→Q+): SR 0→0 0X, 0→1 10, 1→0 01, 1→1 X0. JK 0X, 1X, X1, X0. T 0, 1, 1, 0. D = Q+.
• Race-around: JK with J = K = 1 and pulse width > propagation delay; fix with edge triggering or master–slave (master on CLK = 1, slave on CLK = 0).
theory.Triggering:
• Level triggered: active while clock high (or low). Edge: on the rising (positive) or falling (negative) transition.
• Symbol: triangle = edge; triangle + bubble = negative edge.
theory.Conversions:
• Method: required FF's characteristic table + available FF's excitation table → K-map each input.
• SR→D: S = D, R = D'. JK→D: J = D, K = D'. JK→T: J = K = T. JK→SR: J = S, K = R.
• SR→JK: S = JQ', R = KQ. SR→T: S = TQ', R = TQ.
• T→JK: T = JQ' + KQ. T→D: T = D⊕Q. D→T: D = T⊕Q. D→JK: D = JQ' + K'Q.
theory.Counters:
• n flip-flops → 2ⁿ states (0 … 2ⁿ−1). Mod-N needs the smallest k with 2^k ≥ N. Count after p pulses = p mod N. Cascaded mod-M and mod-N → mod-(M·N).
• Ripple (asynchronous): clock only to the first FF; each output clocks the next; delay n·tpd; f_max = 1/(n·tpd); slower, simpler.
• Synchronous: common clock; faster; any sequence possible.
• Negative edge + clock from Q → up counter; from Q' → down (positive edge reverses this).
theory.Registers:
• n flip-flops store n bits; all shift registers use D flip-flops.
• Clock pulses to load and read n bits: SISO 2n−1, SIPO n, PISO n, PIPO 1.
• Shift left ×2, shift right ÷2. Universal shift register (74194): left, right, parallel load.
• Ring counter: Q of last → first; n states. Johnson (twisted ring): Q' of last → first; 2n states. Unused: 2ⁿ − n and 2ⁿ − 2n.
